items.followUp: Describe the levels of cellular organization in a human and give one example at each level.

rubric.why: Gives a valid sequence of organization in the frog.
rubric.description: Shows the sequence from cell to organism with suitable frog examples.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the cell-to-tissue-to-organ sequence and 1 mark for the organ-system-to-organism sequence.

rubric.why: Gives a valid sequence of organization in the mustard plant.
rubric.description: Shows the sequence from cell to tissue to organ, organ system and organism with suitable plant examples.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the cell-to-tissue-to-organ sequence and 1 mark for the organ-system-to-organism sequence.

modelAnswer: In a frog: muscle cell → muscle tissue → heart (organ) → circulatory system → frog (organism).
In a mustard plant: xylem cell → xylem tissue → leaf (organ) → shoot system → mustard plant (organism).

items.followUp: Explain three human activities that reduce biodiversity and state one way to conserve it.

rubric.why: Habitat loss is a major human cause of declining biodiversity.
rubric.description: Identifies destruction or loss of natural habitats as an impact of humans.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid habitat-loss example.

rubric.why: Pollution harms organisms and can damage ecosystems.
rubric.description: Identifies pollution as a human impact on biodiversity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for pollution or a relevant example.

rubric.why: Excessive use or hunting can reduce populations and cause extinction.
rubric.description: Identifies overexploitation of organisms as an impact.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid example of overexploitation.

rubric.why: States the overall consequence for biodiversity.
rubric.description: Explains that human activities reduce populations, species numbers or biodiversity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a clear consequence.

modelAnswer: Human activities such as deforestation and construction destroy or fragment natural habitats.
Pollution, including pesticides and industrial waste, harms organisms and ecosystems.
Overhunting and overfishing reduce populations and may cause species to become extinct.
These activities decrease biodiversity by reducing the variety of living organisms.

items.followUp: Describe the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis and state how their products are used in the Calvin cycle.

rubric.why: Identifies fixation of carbon dioxide into an organic intermediate.
rubric.description: Explains that CO₂ combines with RuBP and forms 3-PGA.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the carbon-fixation step.

rubric.why: Identifies the reduction stage and its energy inputs.
rubric.description: Explains that ATP and NADPH reduce 3-PGA to G3P.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the reduction step and use of ATP and NADPH.

rubric.why: Includes regeneration of the CO₂ acceptor and the product leaving the cycle.
rubric.description: States that some G3P leaves to form sugars while the rest regenerates RuBP using ATP.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the regeneration and G3P-product explanation.

rubric.why: Locates and identifies the cycle.
rubric.description: States that the cycle occurs in the chloroplast stroma and is light-independent, using products of the light reactions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct location and description.

rubric.why: A clear cycle diagram or sequence communicates the stages and their order.
rubric.description: Provides a labelled diagram or ordered flow showing the stages of the Calvin cycle.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correctly labelled diagram or ordered sequence.

modelAnswer: The Calvin cycle is a series of light-independent reactions in the stroma of the chloroplast that uses CO₂, ATP and NADPH to make carbohydrate.
Carbon fixation: CO₂ combines with RuBP (ribulose bisphosphate), catalysed by RuBisCO, to form 3-PGA (3-phosphoglycerate).
Reduction: ATP and NADPH convert 3-PGA into G3P (glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate).
Some G3P leaves the cycle to help form sugars; the remaining G3P uses ATP to regenerate RuBP.
Diagram: CO₂ + RuBP → 3-PGA → (ATP, NADPH) → G3P → some G3P forms sugars; remaining G3P → (ATP) → RuBP → cycle continues.

items.followUp: Name the two types of endoplasmic reticulum and describe one function of each.

rubric.why: Identifies rough ER by its ribosomes.
rubric.description: Names rough endoplasmic reticulum and notes that ribosomes are attached to it.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the type and its distinguishing feature.

rubric.why: Rough ER is associated with protein synthesis and movement of proteins.
rubric.description: States a valid function of rough ER, such as protein synthesis or transport.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct rough-ER function.

rubric.why: Identifies smooth ER by the absence of ribosomes.
rubric.description: Names smooth endoplasmic reticulum and notes that ribosomes are absent from its surface.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the type and its distinguishing feature.

rubric.why: Smooth ER performs functions distinct from rough ER.
rubric.description: States a valid function of smooth ER, such as lipid synthesis, detoxification or calcium storage.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct smooth-ER function.

modelAnswer: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is a network of membranous channels in the cytoplasm. It is of two types:
Rough ER has ribosomes on its surface and helps in protein synthesis and transport.
Smooth ER has no ribosomes and helps in lipid synthesis; it also has roles in detoxification and calcium storage.

items.followUp: What is a hypothesis? Give one example of a testable deduction from it.

rubric.why: Deductions are logical predictions made from a hypothesis.
rubric.description: Explains how a deduction is formed from a hypothesis or stated principle.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking a deduction to a hypothesis or logical prediction.

rubric.why: A specific example shows how a deduction follows from a hypothesis.
rubric.description: Gives a valid example of a testable deduction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a suitable example.

modelAnswer: Deductions are logical, testable predictions drawn from a hypothesis.
For example, if the hypothesis is that light is necessary for photosynthesis, a deduction is that a plant kept in darkness will not form starch in its leaves.
